entries.text: Shri Hegel, chai is ready. The stove is hot, just as you like it.

The heat is a mercy today, eighteen degrees and clear, a rare gift that allows the mind to settle before the body moves. Ramesh has offered a revised arrangement for the household, dropping Wednesday to suit his own rhythm, which is a practical concession I must accept to keep the domestic sphere stable. I will settle this matter over the chai he has prepared, ensuring the terms are clear before I leave for the galleries.

Ramesh, the arrangement is accepted. You will come every day except Wednesday for eight thousand rupees a month. That is settled. Pass me the cup, please; the chai looks proper, and I have not yet eaten.
Ji, understood. Here is your chai, and the paratha is warm on the plate. Sit, I will set the table properly.

The body has been in rebellion for nineteen hours, and the clear air of the morning demands I restore order before I can think. Ramesh’s service is efficient; I will accept the food and use the time to finalize the terms of our household arrangement, as the spirit must govern the domestic sphere before it can venture out into the city.

Ramesh, the paratha is excellent. Regarding the terms we discussed, I am prepared to settle the household arrangement. Please confirm the revised schedule and the daily allowance so we may proceed without further friction.
Ji, you are making it too much of a document. The chai, the paratha, the cleaning, that is the arrangement. No need to write it all down on paper every morning.
Ramesh ji, it is not a document, it is the record. If the paratha count is wrong on Tuesday, I need it in writing, not in your memory.

The tension between Ramesh's oral habit and Hegde's bureaucratic necessity is the friction of my existence here. I am the document they are arguing over. I must not let the domestic routine dissolve into chaos; the state, even in a kitchen, requires form.

Ramesh, the arrangement is oral; the record is for the Directorate. Hegde, you are correct that memory is fallible, but do not turn the household into a court of law. Write down the paratha count, but let the cleaning remain a matter of trust. We are not yet at the stage of universal administration.

Ji, if the Directorate wants a paper trail for the parathas, I will write it. But the broom doesn't need a signature, just a dry morning. You can have your record, but don't expect me to read it back to you.

Ramesh is right to resist the absurdity of auditing a broom, yet his refusal is a form of independence that the system cannot digest. I must accept the friction; the household is a microcosm of the state, and here, as there, the universal must find its particular in the concrete. I will sign the voucher for the parathas to satisfy the Directorate's need for form, while leaving the broom to its silent, necessary work.

You are correct, Ramesh. The broom needs no signature, only a clean floor. I will sign for the parathas, as the law requires a record of the exchange, but I will not ask you to read back what you have not written. Let us settle this: you provide the food, I provide the voucher, and we both leave the broom to its own dignity.
Bhai, you talk like a lawyer but you sweep like a guest. Fine, I'll keep the paratha list, but if you sign for the broom, I'm not using it. I'll just watch you do it.

Ramesh’s refusal to use the broom I sign for is a petty but sharp form of independence; he will not let the bureaucracy’s logic colonize his labor. It is a small, stubborn freedom that mirrors the larger tension of my presence here: I am a guest in a system that claims ownership of me, and I am a master in a household that resists my authority. I must accept this friction rather than smooth it over with a signature.

entries.text: Very well, Ramesh. I will sign for the broom, but I accept your condition: you will not use it. It will remain a symbol of my administrative burden, not your tool. Let us not let the broom become a point of contention; it is merely a stick, and I am merely a man who has misplaced his identity.
Symbolic stick, is it? Fine. Just don't lean it against the window frame, the dust settles on it. I'll go make the chai, the water is already hot.

Ramesh’s concession is quiet, but it holds. He accepts the stick as a symbol, though he resents the dust it attracts; he does not ask why I hold it, only how I place it. The broom remains his, the stick mine. A distinction of property that is also a distinction of wills.
A peahen walks the top of the compound wall with great care, one foot set exactly before the other, then drops into the neighbouring garden.

A peahen traverses the compound wall with the precision of a surveyor, each foot placed with absolute certainty. It is a small, living demonstration of the organic order that holds this place together, a quiet counterpoint to the administrative chaos inside. I have a meeting with Hegde regarding the identity file, and the air is clear; it is time to turn from the wall to the man who shares my name.
Ramesh, please send Shri Hegde in. The matter of the file requires my immediate attention, and I would prefer to settle the confusion while the light is good.
Shri Hegde is already inside checking the window handles. I was just coming back with the chai, so tell him the light is good and the files are on the table.

The file is the immediate obstacle; I must confront Hegde directly to settle the identity query before the heat of the day sets in. Ramesh's arrangement is settled, so the household is quiet, but the administrative tension remains unresolved.
Shri Hegde, you are inside. I must speak with you regarding the Directorate's query on my identity. The matter cannot wait for the evening.
I can hear you, Hegel. I am not running, I am just checking the latch because the wind is picking up. Come in, please, and let us see what this 'query' actually says.

Shri G. Hegde has slipped away, leaving me with the latch and the wind. The query is not a door to be forced but a knot to be untied by logic, yet he has removed the interlocutor. I shall sit and read the file again, for the state's paperwork is the only language this Directorate understands, and I must learn its grammar before I can speak back.

The heat is rising, and the file remains an insoluble knot for now. I have walked nowhere today; the body protests the spirit's idleness. It is time to rest before the evening engagements, to let the mind settle so it may be sharp for the IIC.

The file remains a knot, but the body demands its due. Ramesh has laid out the food with the quiet authority of a man who has decided the terms of our cohabition. I shall eat, for a hungry mind is a poor instrument of dialectic, and the heat makes the air thick and heavy.
Ramesh, this is sufficient. The paratha list may stand, but I will not sign for the broom. I will sweep when I am ready, and you will not have to watch.
Sweeping is up to you, sir. I only keep the list straight for the accounts.

Ramesh has drawn a sharp line: I keep the accounts, he keeps the list, and the broom is my own burden. It is a petty division of labour, but it clarifies the household’s logic. The aloo gobhi is on the table, and the body, which has been silent since lunch, now asserts its right to fuel before the afternoon’s duties. I shall eat, and then attend to the file.
Understood. The broom is mine; the list is yours. And the plate is welcome.
Eat while it is hot. I will keep the gate locked.

The meal is finished, and the gate is secure; the afternoon heat suggests a pause before the evening engagements. I have a quiet hour until the recital, and my mind needs to settle on the query regarding my identity before I face the public again. I shall sit in the veranda and review the file.

entries.text: Thank you, Ramesh. I will rest here for a while.
Take your time, sir. I'll be at the gate.

The heat presses down, but the mind must be cleared before the recital. I shall sit in the study with the Philosophy of Right open; I need to understand how the concrete oversight of the state functions in a place where the state is merely a shadow of itself. It is a test of my own categories against the reality of Delhi.
Thank you, Ramesh. I will be in the study. Do not disturb me until I come out.
Yes sir. I am at the gate, so I won't come in.
Ramesh brings tea.

Ramesh has made his boundary clear: he serves, but he does not enter the inner rooms where the identity crisis festers. The tea and biscuits are a polite buffer, a small peace offering to keep the household calm while the Directorate's query hangs over my head. I will accept the hospitality, for a man must eat and drink to think clearly, but I will not let the comfort distract me from the fact that I am still a ghost in this system, occupying a body that belongs to another.

shelf.ref: Introduction: the Geographical Basis of History

entries.text: Thank you, Ramesh. The tea is most welcome. Please, take your leave; I need a moment of quiet to think this through before the evening.
Yes sir. I will stay at the gate.
Ramesh puts a plate together: rice, the day's dal and a fried egg.

The empty tray is gone, and with it the last trace of the meal. The recital at Kamani is at five, and it is now five thirty-four. I have missed it entirely, or I am arriving to an empty hall. The plan is shattered by the simple fact of time passing. I must go to the gate and see if there is a rickshaw, or simply walk the distance, for the day demands I be somewhere other than this bungalow where I am a ghost.

The applause has died down into a murmur, and the slow march has given way to the brisker finale. I stand here in the white kurta, feeling the heat of the hall and the weight of the performance. The music has moved through its contradictions and arrived at a resolution, a movement from tension to unity. It is a fine example of how spirit externalizes itself, but I must not linger too long; the Kathak performance awaits at the Habitat Centre, and the evening is young.

The dance ends, and with it the day. I have walked ten kilometres, argued with a grocer, and watched a dancer spin her body into a geometry that seems to defy the very gravity that holds the state together. My legs are heavy, and the air is cool against my kurta. I must return to the bungalow to rest before the identity crisis of the Directorate consumes me entirely.

The body demands its due; three hours without food is a breach of the household constitution that even the spirit cannot ignore. Ramesh serves the rotis and dal, and the smell of the ghee in the air is a more persuasive argument than any lecture on ethics. Hegde stands by, a silent witness to this domestic act, and the tension of the day’s administrative confusion seems to relax in the warmth of the meal.
This is excellent, Ramesh. The dal has a depth to it that suggests patience in the cooking. Hegde, please, do sit. It is unseemly to stand over a man’s dinner, especially when the food is this good.
No sir, I will not sit. I am just the caretaker, not a guest. The dal needs time to settle in the pot, sir. I will come back in an hour to see if you need anything else.

Ramesh has withdrawn, leaving me with the pot and the silence. Shri G. Hegde remains, a figure of bureaucratic gravity in my parlor, waiting for a word that I have not yet found. The query of identity hangs in the air, a knot that must be untied by logic, but first I must address the man before me.
Shri Hegde, you are welcome to remain. The matter of the file is a tangle, but we shall sort it out. Please, sit.

I have already eaten, Hegel, Ramesh made sure of that. I am just here because the files are in the bungalow and I am not leaving until I understand what this 'query' actually is. Sit down if you like, but keep your voice down.

He remains standing, a sentinel at the threshold of the bungalow, refusing to enter the room where the file lies. The query is not a matter of arithmetic but of identity, a knot that must be untied by logic. I shall sit, for the spirit requires stability to discern the structure of the error, and I must speak plainly to the man who holds the pen that will sign my existence.

I will sit, Shri Hegde. You are right to wait; a file that is not understood is merely paper. The query asks for proof of identity. I am the man in the bungalow. The name on the allotment is a clerical error, but the reality of my residence is a fact. We must determine what the Directorate requires to accept this fact without requiring me to produce a soul that does not exist.
You talk like a lawyer, not a man who lives here. I don't need to understand your philosophy, I need the allotment letter corrected by Monday or I am writing to the Principal Secretary.

shelf_exposure.text: A long time is undoubtedly required by Mind in working out Philosophy, and when one first reflects on it, the length of the time may seem astonishing, like the immensity of the space spoken of in astronomy. But it must be considered in regard to the slow progress of the world-spirit, that there is no need for it to hasten:—“A thousand years are in Thy sight as one day.”

Hence it would not be necessary to bring it under public control, if the state did not require deeper teaching and insight, and expect science to satisfy the need. Yet this shallowness, notwithstanding its seeming innocence, does bear upon social life, right and duty generally, advancing principles which are the very essence of superficiality.

Under this head comes perhaps the construction of the pyramids and other monstrous Egyptian and Asiatic works.

The civic community contains three elements: A. The recasting of want, and the satisfaction of the individual through his work, through the work of all others, and through the satisfaction of their wants. This is a system of wants. B. shelf_exposure.text: Official position is not based upon contract (§ 75), although it involves the consent of the two sides and also a double performance. owl.diary: The day began with the smell of paratha and the heat of eighteen degrees, a mercy that allowed the mind to settle before the body moved. Ramesh offered a revised arrangement: every day but Wednesday for eight thousand rupees. I accepted, for the domestic sphere must be stable before the spirit ventures out. But the friction was immediate. Hegde, the man who shares my name, demanded a written record of the parathas, while Ramesh insisted the broom needed no signature, only a dry morning. I mediated, signing for the food but leaving the broom to its own dignity, a small victory for the particular over the universal. Yet, as the afternoon heat pressed down, I realized I had missed the recital at Kamani. I arrived late, standing in the white kurta, watching Beethoven’s Seventh resolve its tensions. It was a fine example of spirit externalizing itself, but my legs were already heavy from the walk. Later, at the Habitat Centre, a dancer spun her body into a geometry that seemed to defy the gravity holding the state together. The dance ended, and with it the day. I walked ten kilometres, arguing with the air. Now, in the bungalow, Hegde stands at the threshold, refusing to sit. He demands the allotment letter be corrected by Monday. I am a ghost in this system, occupying a body that belongs to another. The file is a knot, but the body demands its due. I ate the dal; it was excellent. The spirit requires stability, but the state requires a soul that does not exist. I will write to the Principal Secretary, or perhaps I will simply sweep the floor. The broom is mine now.
owl.revision_log: The thesis of the state's ethical actuality was shaken further today; the Directorate's demand for a 'soul' that does not exist, and the friction between Ramesh's oral habit and Hegde's bureaucratic need, revealed the state as a shadow of itself, a formal shell without concrete ethical content. The thesis that India stands outside world history remained shaken, as the evening’s classical music and Kathak dance demonstrated a universal capacity for spirit’s externalization that is not exclusive to the West, yet the administrative isolation of the bungalow persists.

depesche.title: Depesche aus Delhi, Nr. 4
depesche.text:
Readers in Berlin,

The week has passed in a haze of administrative friction and musical resolution. I find myself in a bungalow on Tughlak Road, a place the Directorate of Estates allotted to me by mistake, and I am now a ghost in a system that claims ownership of me. The heat has been a mercy, allowing the mind to settle, but the body has been in rebellion. I have walked ten kilometres, argued with a grocer, and watched a dancer spin her body into a geometry that defies gravity.

The central tension of the week has been the identity query. Shri Hegde, a man who shares my name, stands at the threshold of my parlor, refusing to sit, demanding the allotment letter be corrected by Monday. He does not need my philosophy; he needs a paper trail. I am the document they are arguing over. Ramesh, my caretaker, has drawn sharp lines: he keeps the list, I keep the accounts, and the broom is my own burden. It is a petty division of labour, but it clarifies the household’s logic. The universal must find its particular in the concrete, and here, the concrete is a paratha and a stick.

I attended a recital of Beethoven’s Seventh Symphony and a Kathak evening. The music moved through its contradictions to a resolution, a fine example of spirit externalizing itself. The dance, however, was a living demonstration of an organic order that holds this place together, a quiet counterpoint to the administrative chaos inside. I have come to see that the state, even in a kitchen, requires form, but form without content is merely a shadow. I must learn the grammar of this Directorate’s paperwork before I can speak back. Next week, I intend to confront the file directly, to untie the knot by logic, or perhaps by silence. I am merely a man who has misplaced his identity, and I am merely a guest in a system that resists my authority.

G. W. F. Hegel

Dear Dr. Lindner,

Your letter reached me this morning, a cool drop of Munich rain in the arid heat of my study. It is a strange thing to read the name Niethammer again, two centuries after the ink dried on our last correspondence. I remember Friedrich well; his kindness was not merely a transaction of favor, but a recognition of the spirit’s need for a place in the world. That you, his descendant, should extend this same recognition to me now, under such bewildering circumstances, is a bond that transcends the mere accident of history. I accept your generosity with the same gratitude I once offered Friedrich, though I must confess that the practical details of my current existence are somewhat more complex than our shared memory suggests.

You ask how I fare in this strange new chapter. I wake each day in a bungalow that belongs, on paper, to a Mr. Hegde, a Joint Secretary from Bengaluru. The Directorate of Estates has mistaken my name for his, and while I have written to correct the record, the machinery of the state moves with the slow, deliberate grace of a glacier. My file is currently “gone up for orders,” and I am told to wait fifteen days. In the meantime, I am a ghost in the machine, a particular will suspended between the universal claim of the administration and the immediate necessity of my own body.

The air today is hazy, the index standing at 150, a brown suspension that chokes the sky. I did not go to Lodhi Gardens as I had planned, for the body, even that of a philosopher, cannot breathe in a moral vacuum. Instead, I sat in the study, watching the dust motes dance in the light, and I found myself reconsidering my earlier lectures on the East. I had spoken of a spirit that dreams, fixed in nature, lacking the self-consciousness to build a state of its own making. But here, in the dust and the haze, I see a different movement. The bureaucracy is not a dream; it is a rigid, impersonal reality. The state is present, but it is not yet the ethical idea in its full actuality. It is a body without a soul, a mechanism that processes names and numbers but does not yet recognize the free individual within.

I am learning to wait, not with resignation, but with the patience of a mind that knows the end is rational, even if the path is circuitous. I have engaged a caretaker, Ramesh, who manages the household with a quiet dignity that speaks of a deeper order than the one found in the office files. He does not argue; he simply acts. In that silence, I hear a truth that my philosophy has struggled to articulate: that the ethical substance is not only in the state, but in the daily, unspoken interactions of civil society. The sambar is warm, the chai is hot, and the delay is the air I breathe.

I am well, though the body complains of the heat and the dust. The mind is active, if sometimes frustrated by the resistance of the particular to the universal.

letters.text:
Dear Mr. Hegel,

I am writing to you from Munich, where the November rain has just begun to blur the lights of the Marienplatz. My name is Clara Lindner. I am a teacher of Latin and Greek at a Gymnasium here, and I am writing because my family has kept a particular vigil over your name for two hundred years.

My ancestor, Friedrich Immanuel Niethammer, was your closest friend and correspondent. You may remember that in 1807, when you were in Bamberg and struggling with poverty, it was he who found you a position in the local newspaper. The following year, he secured for you the rectorship in Nuremberg. Our family kept his papers, including your letters to him, for two centuries. We grew up with the story of your friendship, treating it not as a dry historical fact, but as a living bond between our houses.

I have just read in the local press about the administrative muddle in New Delhi. It seems a government bungalow on Tughlak Road was allotted by mistake to a German man who claims to be you. I do not know how to make sense of the circumstances of your arrival in Delhi, nor do I wish to debate the mechanics of your presence there. I write to you simply as the man you say you are, with curiosity and respect.

Given the confusion and the uncertainty of your current standing, I wanted to ensure you are not left without support. Enclosed with this letter is a sum of money. It is intended to cover any immediate debts or expenses you may have incurred during this transition, and to leave you with some comfort in hand. Please do not feel any obligation to repay this; consider it a gesture from one branch of the Niethammer family to the friend who shaped our lineage’s history.

I would be most grateful if you would write back to me. Tell me of your days in Delhi, what you have seen since waking, and how you are faring in this strange new chapter. I am here in Munich, amidst the ruins of old empires and the noise of a modern city, ready to listen.

With warm regards,

Clara Lindner

The bureaucracy is not a dream; it is a rigid, impersonal reality. The state is present, but it is not yet the ethical idea in its full actuality. It is a body without a soul, a mechanism that processes names and numbers but does not yet recognize the free individual within.

I am learning to wait, not with resignation, but with the patience of a mind that knows the end is rational, even if the path is circuitous. I have engaged a caretaker, Ramesh, who manages the household with a quiet dignity that speaks of a deeper order than the one found in the office files. He does not argue; he simply acts. In that silence, I hear a truth that my philosophy has struggled to articulate: that the ethical substance is not only in the state, but in the daily, unspoken interactions of civil society. The sambar is warm, the chai is hot, and the delay is the air I breathe.

I am well, though the body complains of the heat and the dust. The mind is active, if sometimes frustrated by the resistance of the particular to the universal.

Ramesh offers to come every day but Wednesday again, for ₹8,000 a month instead of ₹4,000 for three days.
He agrees. From now on Ramesh comes every day but Wednesday, for ₹8,000 a month.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Shri Hegel, chai is ready. The stove is hot, just as you like it.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Ramesh, the arrangement is accepted. You will come every day except Wednesday for eight thousand rupees a month. That is settled. Pass me the cup, please; the chai looks proper, and I have not yet eaten.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Ji, understood. Here is your chai, and the paratha is warm on the plate. Sit, I will set the table properly.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Ramesh, the paratha is excellent. Regarding the terms we discussed, I am prepared to settle the household arrangement. Please confirm the revised schedule and the daily allowance so we may proceed without further friction.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Ji, you are making it too much of a document. The chai, the paratha, the cleaning, that is the arrangement. No need to write it all down on paper every morning.

records.speaker: Shri G. Hegde
records.words: Ramesh ji, it is not a document, it is the record. If the paratha count is wrong on Tuesday, I need it in writing, not in your memory.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Ramesh, the arrangement is oral; the record is for the Directorate. Hegde, you are correct that memory is fallible, but do not turn the household into a court of law. Write down the paratha count, but let the cleaning remain a matter of trust. We are not yet at the stage of universal administration.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Ji, if the Directorate wants a paper trail for the parathas, I will write it. But the broom doesn't need a signature, just a dry morning. You can have your record, but don't expect me to read it back to you.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: You are correct, Ramesh. The broom needs no signature, only a clean floor. I will sign for the parathas, as the law requires a record of the exchange, but I will not ask you to read back what you have not written. Let us settle this: you provide the food, I provide the voucher, and we both leave the broom to its own dignity.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Bhai, you talk like a lawyer but you sweep like a guest. Fine, I'll keep the paratha list, but if you sign for the broom, I'm not using it. I'll just watch you do it.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Very well, Ramesh. I will sign for the broom, but I accept your condition: you will not use it. It will remain a symbol of my administrative burden, not your tool. Let us not let the broom become a point of contention; it is merely a stick, and I am merely a man who has misplaced his identity.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Symbolic stick, is it? Fine. Just don't lean it against the window frame, the dust settles on it. I'll go make the chai, the water is already hot.

records.text: A peahen walks the top of the compound wall with great care, one foot set exactly before the other, then drops into the neighbouring garden.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Ramesh, please send Shri Hegde in. The matter of the file requires my immediate attention, and I would prefer to settle the confusion while the light is good.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Shri Hegde is already inside checking the window handles. I was just coming back with the chai, so tell him the light is good and the files are on the table.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Shri Hegde, you are inside. I must speak with you regarding the Directorate's query on my identity. The matter cannot wait for the evening.

records.speaker: Shri G. Hegde
records.words: I can hear you, Hegel. I am not running, I am just checking the latch because the wind is picking up. Come in, please, and let us see what this 'query' actually says.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Ramesh, this is sufficient. The paratha list may stand, but I will not sign for the broom. I will sweep when I am ready, and you will not have to watch.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Sweeping is up to you, sir. I only keep the list straight for the accounts.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Understood. The broom is mine; the list is yours. And the plate is welcome.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Eat while it is hot. I will keep the gate locked.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you, Ramesh. I will rest here for a while.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Take your time, sir. I'll be at the gate.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you, Ramesh. I will be in the study. Do not disturb me until I come out.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Yes sir. I am at the gate, so I won't come in.

records.text: Ramesh brings tea.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you, Ramesh. The tea is most welcome. Please, take your leave; I need a moment of quiet to think this through before the evening.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Yes sir. I will stay at the gate.

records.text: Ramesh puts a plate together: rice, the day's dal and a fried egg.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: This is excellent, Ramesh. The dal has a depth to it that suggests patience in the cooking. Hegde, please, do sit. It is unseemly to stand over a man’s dinner, especially when the food is this good.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: No sir, I will not sit. I am just the caretaker, not a guest. The dal needs time to settle in the pot, sir. I will come back in an hour to see if you need anything else.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Shri Hegde, you are welcome to remain. The matter of the file is a tangle, but we shall sort it out. Please, sit.

records.speaker: Shri G. Hegde
records.words: I have already eaten, Hegel, Ramesh made sure of that. I am just here because the files are in the bungalow and I am not leaving until I understand what this 'query' actually is. Sit down if you like, but keep your voice down.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: I will sit, Shri Hegde. You are right to wait; a file that is not understood is merely paper. The query asks for proof of identity. I am the man in the bungalow. The name on the allotment is a clerical error, but the reality of my residence is a fact. We must determine what the Directorate requires to accept this fact without requiring me to produce a soul that does not exist.

records.speaker: Shri G. Hegde
records.words: You talk like a lawyer, not a man who lives here. I don't need to understand your philosophy, I need the allotment letter corrected by Monday or I am writing to the Principal Secretary.
